Johnson tells Katzenbach he wants the matter left to ordinary processes: an FBI report to the Attorney General and a Texas court of inquiry.
Johnson calls Hoover. The FBI then lobbies the Washington Post, successfully, to drop a planned editorial backing a presidential commission.
Lawyers Jim Martin and Tom Howard, roommate George Senator, and reporters Bill Hunter and Jim Koethe meet in Ruby's apartment.

A Mexico City operator reports overhearing a call saying "the Castro plan is being carried out" and that Bobby Kennedy is next. The numbers trace to Batista-era UN ambassador Emilio Núñez Portuondo, later described as a CIA asset, and a Mexico City investigator; the Secret Service never interviews the latter and closes the case.
Kennedy's funeral in Washington. Theodore White later regrets his "Camelot" framing; Salinger and Roger Hilsman dismiss it as a myth.

Agent Jerry Blaine reports the Elms incident to Chief Rowley, who reportedly asks who ordered agents off the limousine's rear in Dallas; agents say Kennedy himself gave that order in Tampa. The FBI learns Ferrie's library card was said to be on Oswald. Corpsman Dennis David later says he found Lt. Cmdr. Pitzer editing film and slides of the President's body, and that both concluded the fatal shot entered the forehead. Daniel Marvin later claims the CIA asked him in 1965 to kill Pitzer, who was found shot in 1966, ruled a suicide.
An agitated Johnson calls Hoover about the Post editorial and a possible commission; the White House announces Hoover will investigate.
Johnson tells columnist Joseph Alsop that another commission would mean people running over each other.
Kennedy's body leaves the Capitol Rotunda.

At the Fort Worth funeral home, director Paul Groody says the FBI fingerprinted Oswald's body; agent Richard Harrison says he drove another agent there with the rifle, to put Oswald's palm print on it "for comparison purposes."
Oswald is buried at Rose Hill Cemetery under the cover name "William Bobo"; a reluctant minister presides and reporters serve as pallbearers.

An FBI teletype records Gill telling Ferrie's roommate about the library card. Hoover tells Johnson he has killed a Post story about a presidential report. Ferrie returns and, with Gill, is questioned by the DA; he denies lending Oswald his card, then is said to rush to Oswald's old neighborhood asking about it.
The library card is never explained; the chronology suggests that if a Dallas officer tipped off Gill (Marcello's lawyer) and destroyed it, that would link police to Marcello.
Dr. Jack Harper reports that his nephew found a piece of skull in Dealey Plaza; the Secret Service wants it sent to the White House, but the FBI's Belmont has it sent to the FBI lab.
A CIA document relays a report describing the weapon as a Model 91 rifle, calling it a Mauser.
The Dallas Morning News reports Oswald met the FBI on November 16.
A man calling himself Harry Power leaves a 6.5mm Carcano at a Terre Haute hotel; the Secret Service takes the rifle and the case goes to the Warren Commission.
Records link Power to the Walker shooting inquiry, other files call his rifle a Mauser, and Richard Nagell later tells Garrison investigators Power knew Oswald.
Gilberto Policarpo Lopez checks into the Roosevelt Hotel in Mexico City.
Robert Kennedy asks Daniel Patrick Moynihan to look into whether Hoffa was involved and whether the Secret Service had been bought.

Acting on a tip, the FBI finds a repair tag at the Irving Sports Shop for scope work for "Oswald." Gunsmith Dial Ryder says he never worked on a Carcano, and the tag shows three mounting holes where Oswald's rifle needed two, suggesting an impersonator.

Katzenbach writes Bill Moyers that the public must be satisfied Oswald was the assassin with no confederates, that speculation must be cut off, that the facts seem "too pat," and that a full FBI report should be released. Aides say Johnson suspected Cuban involvement, linked to CIA plots against Castro.

Richard Helms recalls Johnson worried into 1964 about a conspiracy. Dallas radio supervisor J.C. Bowles says federal agents borrowed the original police Dictabelts, he believed for a studio in Oklahoma.
In his first FBI interview, Ruby says he acted alone to spare the Kennedy family a trial.
HSCA polygraph experts later find Ruby's polygraph badly run, yet his reaction to "Did you assist Oswald?" suggests he may have been lying.

A Ford glass-plant employee later tells Douglas Weldon he saw the limousine's windshield, with a hole through it from the outside, being used as a template for a replacement; the windshield given to the Warren Commission has no hole.
After the funeral, Johnson receives some 220 foreign leaders at the State Department.

A Hoover memo says the FBI intercepted Oswald's letter to the Soviet Embassy, addressed to an official said to handle assassinations, and that airing it publicly would "muddy the waters internationally."
Kansas radio newsman Raymond Carnay tells a Dallas officer Oswald tried to win him over to Castro in Dallas in 1961, when Oswald was in Minsk.
The New York Times reports, citing a Laredo customs official, that Oswald's movements into Mexico were watched at a federal agency's request.

Karin Kupcinet, daughter of a Ruby acquaintance, is found murdered; she is said to have been overheard speaking of the assassination beforehand. The FBI interviews Ferrie, who denies knowing Oswald but describes work for Marcello's defense, including trips to Guatemala and meetings on November 9 and 16.
Ford's Ferguson returns; on Secret Service instructions, glaziers push out the cracked windshield, which is locked away. Ferguson notes a dent in the windshield's chrome trim.

Lead fragments from the crack are later tested; the Warren Report says the windshield damage and chrome dent were caused by fragments, not the bullet that exited the President's neck. Greer and Kellerman did not notice the dent before Dallas.
Jack Martin tells FBI agent Regis Kennedy he saw rifles like Oswald's at Ferrie's apartment and that Ferrie, an amateur hypnotist, should be examined.
Police officer Fred O'Sullivan tells the FBI Oswald attended a couple of Lakefront Civil Air Patrol meetings when Ferrie was squadron commander, but he cannot say they met.

Gilberto Alvarado tells the CIA he saw Oswald recruited at the Cuban Consulate on September 18, when Oswald was still in New Orleans; he retracts on November 30. His story may have delayed the FBI report.
Johnson tells Rep. Charles Halleck the matter has foreign implications and could cost 39 million lives if Khrushchev or Castro were blamed; he wants the Chief Justice to lead it.
Johnson reportedly tells Kennedy aide Ralph Dungan that Kennedy's death was "divine retribution" for Diem's murder.
Ferrie suggests the FBI ask CAP instructor Jerry Paradis; Paradis later tells the HSCA Oswald attended at least 10 or 15 Lakefront meetings.
Robert Kennedy and Mrs. Kennedy visit the grave alone.
Johnson moves into the Oval Office; the stock market posts a record rebound.
Robert Kennedy speaks privately with Clint Hill; no record survives.
Hoover tells McCone the FBI wants to dispel rumors and that Oswald is "the right man." Sen. Richard Russell lunches with Johnson for 75 minutes, unrecorded.

Johnson approves NSAM 273 on Vietnam. A draft dated November 21 was found in 1991. McNamara later writes that Kennedy would probably have withdrawn; whether NSAM 273 reversed Kennedy's policy is debated.
Ambassador Thomas Mann cables fears of Cuban involvement and starts his own inquiry, but the White House stops it.
Ruby is charged with murder with malice.
Flying with Lt. Francis Fruge, Rose Cheramie laughs at a headline saying no link between Ruby and Oswald had been found, claiming from her time at Ruby's club that the two were close.
An inventory of Oswald's things from the Paine house lists a Minox camera, later changed to "light meter"; the chronology suggests the camera pointed to intelligence ties.

Sibert and O'Neill dictate their autopsy report. O'Sullivan tells the FBI Ferrie took over the Moisant CAP unit around when Oswald may have joined. County surveyor Robert West makes the first plat of Dealey Plaza, for Time-Life.

Burkley receives the autopsy report from agent Bouck. Mrs. R.E. Arnold tells the FBI she saw Oswald on the Depository's first floor around 12:15–12:20; a later FBI statement has her say otherwise, and she is not called as a witness.
The rifle goes to Washington again; Dallas police only now give the FBI the four Tippit-scene cartridge cases.
Marina Oswald refuses an FBI interview because Hosty is present. Agent Mike Howard recalls Johnson ordering that no one talk to the family; a guard is given a submachine gun.

Press reports cite customs officials saying Oswald's Mexico crossings were monitored and that Immigration had a folder on his trip; the Warren Report does not mention them. Texas announces, then three days later drops, a state inquiry.
Ford's Ferguson first appears in the White House garage log; he later says his work began November 23 and drives the limousine to Dearborn on December 20.

Hosty collects Oswald's notebook and other items from Fritz at 1 AM. The FBI's transcript for the Warren Commission retypes two pages and omits the notation of Hosty's name and number; one page is cut out.
A grand jury indicts Ruby. The FBI questions and releases Joseph Milteer, who denies threatening the President.
Sibert and O'Neill interview agents Kellerman, Greer and Behn.
Policarpo Lopez flies to Havana as the only passenger on a nine-crew flight. The HSCA calls his case troubling and unresolved.
Johnson addresses Congress, stressing continuity and commitments from South Vietnam to Berlin, and urges a tax cut.
Mrs. Kennedy pays her only visit to Johnson's office.
Robert Kennedy's first private meeting with Johnson lasts twelve minutes, touching on the swearing-in, the delay leaving Dallas and the Oval Office.
At Hickory Hill, Walter Sheridan tells RFK of reports that Hoffa cheered the news; RFK sends him to Dallas to make inquiries, including about Marina.
FBI marksmen fire Oswald's rifle at stationary targets 45 feet away; none fires three shots in 5.6 seconds, and all shoot high and right.
FBI headquarters receives a copy of the Zapruder film, returned December 4.

A Miami informant tells the Secret Service that a Cuban terrorist named Machado was rumored to have been assigned to get Oswald to Cuba; the Warren Commission gets only a summary and there is no follow-up.
FBI headquarters asks Mexico City for any tapes of Oswald's embassy contacts. Congressional and Texas inquiries are proposed; Rostow's suggestion of a commission traces to November 24.
Agents secure Hyannis Port as Mrs. Kennedy and the children visit the grave once more and fly to Cape Cod.

Trooper Hurchel Jacks says the Secret Service told them to stop photographs of the car's interior. Sheriff Decker declines to discuss the case with the FBI. Marguerite Oswald is released from Secret Service custody but kept from seeing Marina again.
Silvia Odio tells a friend and her psychiatrist she knew Oswald from exile meetings and had heard he might be a double agent; the friend tells the FBI.
Alvarado is interrogated at a CIA safe house; the FBI says Oswald was in New Orleans on the date he gave.

The New Orleans FBI closes its inquiry into Martin's allegations, calling him unreliable. Ferrie admits criticizing Kennedy over the Bay of Pigs and perhaps saying "he ought to be shot," but denies any plan.
The Secret Service calls Martin's claims about Ferrie training Oswald "without foundation."
The Secret Service reports three shots: the first and third hit the President, the second hit Connally.
An Italian military intelligence report, obtained by the FBI and CIA, describes the weapon as a Model 91 rifle.
Johnson asks Sen. James Eastland to shut down a proposed Senate hearing, and succeeds.
Theodore White interviews Mrs. Kennedy alone at Hyannis Port, the origin of the "Camelot" story.
White finishes typing the article at 2 AM.
Johnson creates the President's Commission on the Assassination by Executive Order 11130.

Until now only Texas authorities had legal jurisdiction; killing a President becomes a federal crime only after the Commission recommends it. Hoover tells Johnson the FBI report naming Oswald as lone assassin is almost done.
Hoover tells Johnson all three shots were fired at the President and two splintered bullets were matched to the rifle.
Hoover urges Johnson to get a bulletproof car.
Johnson again tells Halleck the matter has foreign implications, involving the CIA, and could cost 39 million lives.
